title: A Tale of Two HTTP/2 Codecs
excerpt: An Envoy version bump cost a customer 20% of their HTTP/2 throughput. The trail leads through two codecs, a pile of flamegraphs, and the Huffman code hiding inside every header.

EngineeringAug 4, 20268 min read

An Envoy version bump cost a customer 20% of their HTTP/2 throughput. The trail leads through two codecs, a pile of flamegraphs, and the Huffman code hiding inside every header.

Dmitry Ilyevsky

Co-founder & CTO

A while back we rolled a routine Envoy upgrade to one of our customers' dedicated proxies. Same config, same traffic, and the CPU graphs stepped up by roughly a fifth. This is the kind of chart that earns you a calendar invite with no agenda, so we decided to get ahead of it and started digging in.

Bisecting versions pointed at Envoy v1.34, which is where Envoy switched its default HTTP/2 codec from nghttp2 to Google's oghttp2. We weren't the first to notice: users had been reporting 15–25% latency regressions since that release, and v1.37.0 eventually flipped the default back, with a comment in the source promising to try again "once performance aligns with nghttp2." That fixed our customer. It did not fix our curiosity. Why doesn't it align? What does an HTTP/2 codec even spend its time on?

This post is the investigation. There's a sequel coming where we make the fast codec faster still, but first things first.

The best of codecs, the worst of codecs

Envoy has two implementations of HTTP/2 behind a runtime flag, though nobody could say which was which without a flamegraph:

  • nghttp2 - Tatsuhiro Tsujikawa's C library, the HTTP/2 workhorse since 2013 and Envoy's original codec. Lean C structs, caller-provided buffers.
  • oghttp2 - Google's C++ codec from the QUICHE family, which shares code with the HTTP/3 stack. It became Envoy's default in v1.34, and that's when the regression reports started.

We benchmarked both on four microarchitectures (Intel Sapphire Rapids, AMD Zen 4, AWS Graviton4, Google Axion). Setup, briefly: same-host loopback (h2load → Envoy → Go h2c backend, or Envoy serving direct_response), every process pinned to disjoint physical cores, Envoy at --concurrency 1, so RPS/core is a pure CPU-efficiency number.

The user reports reproduce almost exactly: nghttp2 beats oghttp2 by 15–25% RPS/core on header-heavy proxied traffic, on every host, and by 7–19% under heavy connection churn. So the regression is real, portable, and lives somewhere in the codec. Time to open the profiles.

PSA

If you build Envoy yourself, check your optimization flags. Envoy's .bazelrc does not default to -c opt - a plain bazel build //source/exe:envoy-static produces a fastbuild (debug) binary that looks completely functional and benchmarks 15–32× slower per core than the same source at -c opt. Every number in this post is from -c opt builds. We found this out the embarrassing way.

Where an HTTP/2 codec spends its day

The flamegraphs for both codecs are dominated by the same job: header decompression. Every HTTP/2 request that crosses a proxy arrives with its headers compressed, and the proxy has to undo that - twice per hop, decode and re-encode - before it can route anything. It's a few hundred bytes of work per request, which sounds like nothing until you multiply it out: tens of thousands of requests per second per core, a dozen-plus header fields each, so the per-field decode path runs a few hundred thousand times a second.

The compression scheme is HPACK (RFC 7541): two mechanisms working together. The first is indexing: a fixed 61-entry static table covers the universal headers (:method: GET is a single byte), and both sides maintain a synchronized dynamic table of recently seen header fields - so the second time you send cookie: session=abc... it costs one or two bytes instead of the kilobyte it costs literally. The second mechanism handles everything that can't be an index hit: literal strings are Huffman-coded. First-time headers, unique values (request IDs, tokens, the cookie your ad vendor rotates on every request), and most of what crosses a fresh connection goes through the Huffman path. A proxy at the edge sees a lot of fresh connections and a lot of unique values, so this path is hot.

A two-minute tour of Huffman coding

In 1951, Robert Fano offered the students in his MIT information theory course a choice: sit the final exam, or write a term paper on a problem he supplied. One of the problems sounded almost too plain to be worth a grade - given a set of symbols and how often each one occurs, find the most efficient binary code for them. Fano didn't mention that he and Claude Shannon (yes, the Claude Shannon) had both attacked this exact problem and gotten only approximations. A graduate student named David Huffman picked the paper, struggled with it for months, and by his own account had just thrown his notes in the trash to start studying for the exam when the solution surfaced.

Everyone before him had built codes from the top down, splitting the symbol set into halves. Huffman inverted it: start from the bottom - take the two rarest symbols, merge them into one, repeat until a single tree remains. Rare symbols end up deep in the tree with long codes; frequent symbols end up shallow with short ones. That term-paper construction is provably optimal1. Seventy-five years later it sits inside JPEG, gzip, MP3 (for kids, this is like Spotify but without ads) - and every HTTP/2 header on the internet.

HPACK ships one fixed Huffman code for header text, its frequencies baked into the RFC from real header corpora captured a decade ago, so both ends of a connection always agree on it. Lowercase letters and digits sit near the top of the tree at 5–7 bits; rare bytes hang thirty levels deep. Typical header text comes out around 6 bits per byte. Now notice the property the tree structure gives you for free: no codeword can be the beginning of another, because symbols only live at the leaves. So the bit stream needs no delimiters at all. Read bits until they trace a path to a leaf - that's your symbol. Start again from the root. The stream carries its own boundaries, provided you start at the right place.

It also tells you where the cost lives. Encoding is table lookups and bit-appending. Decoding is that walk: left on 0, right on 1, emit at a leaf, jump back to the root - for HPACK's code, an average of ~6 dependent branch-and-load steps per output byte, which is a lot of machinery for one character of a cookie.

Here's the encoding half on a header value - step through it character by character and watch the codes pack into bytes with no regard for byte boundaries:

nghttp2 does something much better, and has since 2014: it decodes with a precomputed finite-state machine. A decoder mid-stream can only be in finitely many states - one per internal node of the Huffman tree, and HPACK's canonical tree has exactly 256 of them, so the state fits in one byte. You can precompute, for every (state, next-n-bits) pair, where you end up and which symbols (if any) you emit along the way. Decoding becomes: take the next n bits, index a table, maybe write a byte, repeat. No bit-buffer, no branching on code lengths.

The machine below decodes an example header value under the standard RFC 7541 code, reading two bits per lookup so the whole state table fits on screen. Step through it - the table and the tree are the same thing wearing different clothes:

nghttp2 runs exactly this machine with 4-bit chunks: two lookups per input byte into a table of 256 states × 16 nibble values - 16 KiB, which sits comfortably in L1 cache. Validity checking (HPACK requires padding to be all-ones, and an embedded end-of-string symbol is an error) folds into the same lookup. It's a genuinely nice piece of engineering - one reason nghttp2's HPACK path profiles so flat.

So oghttp2's Huffman decoder must be the problem, right?

That was our assumption going in, and the profiles said no. QUICHE's Huffman kernel is slower than nghttp2's FSM, but the bulk of the difference sits above the decoder: HttpHeaderBlock and the layers of representation and bookkeeping each decoded header passes through cost a consistent 20–30 µs per request more than nghttp2's path, on every host we measured. One line item stood out: the decoder emits symbols through std::string::push_back, one byte at a time, and that call alone burns 13–20% of all of Envoy's CPU on the x86 hosts in header-saturated runs.

You can see the shape of it in the source. The decoder's hot loop hands every decoded character to std::string individually:

Each push_back is a capacity check and a possible reallocation per byte of header text. Then, once a value is fully decoded, every header goes through a hash-map lookup plus an arena copy before Envoy ever sees it:

Both are perfectly reasonable C++ in isolation. On a path that runs once per header field - a few hundred thousand times per second per core - the reallocation checks, map lookups, and copies add up to the 20–30 µs the profiles show - while nghttp2's decoder writes into a caller-provided buffer and moves on.

To be fair, oghttp2's framing and session layer is cheaper than nghttp2's - in the one scenario where header literals stop dominating (realistic headers, direct response, no proxying), oghttp2 wins by 8–13%. The codec isn't slow everywhere. But a proxy's job description is header-heavy, and on header-heavy traffic the plumbing tax buries the framing win.

The fix upstream needs is a leaner path from decoded bytes to header block, which is a deeper refactor than any single hot loop. That's presumably why the Envoy default got flipped back instead of forward.

The fix

For us and our customers, the fix was pleasantly boring:

  • Envoy 1.37+: you're done; nghttp2 is the default again.
  • Envoy 1.34–1.36: set envoy.reloadable_features.http2_use_oghttp2: false. It's one line of runtime config and it's worth 15–25% RPS/core on most proxied HTTP/2 traffic.

We rolled the flag across our fleet, the customer's graphs stepped back down, so the calendar invite never came (for now). It is a far, far better thing to flip a runtime flag than to refactor a header pipeline so kudos to the Envoy team for leaving the escape hatch.

Conclusions

Codec defaults are performance changes. A minor-version Envoy bump changed our customer's CPU bill by 20% without touching a single byte on the wire. If you operate proxies, benchmark the versions you actually ship. Generating loads representative of real production traffic can be tricky though, we'll write more about that later.

Profile before you optimize. We went in certain the Huffman decoder was the villain, and the flamegraphs pointed at string plumbing instead. The decoder was, if anything, the best part of both codecs.

Header decompression is a substantial workload. A few hundred bytes per request, a dozen header fields each, tens of thousands of requests per second per core, twice per hop - the arithmetic stops being funny quickly. HTTP/2's attempt to save bandwidth can really bite on the CPU usage. Tradeoffs and all...

While we were in there, though, we kept staring at nghttp2's n=4 table and at a 2017 paper by the nghttp2 author and friends that says you can read a whole byte at a time - if you're willing to pay for a table sixteen times larger. Whether that trade survives contact with a CPU cache is the next post. Stay tuned.

blocks.html_en: Where an HTTP/2 codec spends its day

sentences.en: Where an HTTP/2 codec spends its day
sentences.zh: HTTP/2 编解码器的工作场所

blocks.html_en: The flamegraphs for both codecs are dominated by the same job: header decompression. Every HTTP/2 request that crosses a proxy arrives with its headers compressed, and the proxy has to undo that - twice per hop, decode and re-encode - before it can route anything. It's a few hundred bytes of work per request, which sounds like nothing until you multiply it out: tens of thousands of requests per second per core, a dozen-plus header fields each, so the per-field decode path runs a few hundred thousand times a second.

sentences.en: The flamegraphs for both codecs are dominated by the same job: header decompression.
sentences.zh: 两种编解码器的火焰图都由相同的工作主导：标头解压缩。

sentences.en: Every HTTP/2 request that crosses a proxy arrives with its headers compressed, and the proxy has to undo that - twice per hop, decode and re-encode - before it can route anything.
sentences.zh: 每个跨代理的 HTTP/2 请求到达时其标头都已压缩，代理必须撤消该操作（每跳两次、解码并重新编码），然后才能路由任何内容。

sentences.en: It's a few hundred bytes of work per request, which sounds like nothing until you multiply it out: tens of thousands of requests per second per core, a dozen-plus header fields each, so the per-field decode path runs a few hundred thousand times a second.
sentences.zh: 每个请求需要几百个字节的工作量，听起来没什么，除非你将其相乘：每个核心每秒有数万个请求，每个请求有十多个标头字段，因此每个字段的解码路径每秒运行几十万次。

blocks.html_en: The compression scheme is HPACK (RFC 7541): two mechanisms working together. The first is indexing: a fixed 61-entry static table covers the universal headers (:method: GET is a single byte), and both sides maintain a synchronized dynamic table of recently seen header fields - so the second time you send cookie: session=abc... it costs one or two bytes instead of the kilobyte it costs literally. The second mechanism handles everything that can't be an index hit: literal strings are Huffman-coded. First-time headers, unique values (request IDs, tokens, the cookie your ad vendor rotates on every request), and most of what crosses a fresh connection goes through the Huffman path. A proxy at the edge sees a lot of fresh connections and a lot of unique values, so this path is hot.

sentences.en: A two-minute tour of Huffman coding
sentences.zh: 两分钟的霍夫曼编码之旅

blocks.html_en: In 1951, Robert Fano offered the students in his MIT information theory course a choice: sit the final exam, or write a term paper on a problem he supplied. One of the problems sounded almost too plain to be worth a grade - given a set of symbols and how often each one occurs, find the most efficient binary code for them. Fano didn't mention that he and Claude Shannon (yes, the Claude Shannon) had both attacked this exact problem and gotten only approximations. A graduate student named David Huffman picked the paper, struggled with it for months, and by his own account had just thrown his notes in the trash to start studying for the exam when the solution surfaced.

sentences.en: In 1951, Robert Fano offered the students in his MIT information theory course a choice: sit the final exam, or write a term paper on a problem he supplied.
sentences.zh: 1951 年，罗伯特·法诺 (Robert Fano) 为麻省理工学院信息论课程的学生提供了一个选择：参加期末考试，或者就他提供的问题写一篇学期论文。

sentences.en: One of the problems sounded almost too plain to be worth a grade - given a set of symbols and how often each one occurs, find the most efficient binary code for them.

sentences.en: A graduate student named David Huffman picked the paper, struggled with it for months, and by his own account had just thrown his notes in the trash to start studying for the exam when the solution surfaced.
sentences.zh: 一位名叫大卫·霍夫曼（David Huffman）的研究生选择了这张试卷，并为此苦苦挣扎了几个月，据他自己说，当解决方案浮出水面时，他刚刚将笔记扔进垃圾桶，开始准备考试。

blocks.html_en: Everyone before him had built codes from the top down, splitting the symbol set into halves. Huffman inverted it: start from the bottom - take the two rarest symbols, merge them into one, repeat until a single tree remains. Rare symbols end up deep in the tree with long codes; frequent symbols end up shallow with short ones. That term-paper construction is provably optimal1. Seventy-five years later it sits inside JPEG, gzip, MP3 (for kids, this is like Spotify but without ads) - and every HTTP/2 header on the internet.

blocks.html_en: Frequent letters end up shallow with short codes; rare ones hang deep. And because letters live only at the leaves, no code can be the prefix of another - hover a letter to trace its path from the root. The leaves, top to bottom, spell what a decoder does when it reaches one.

sentences.en: Frequent letters end up shallow with short codes; rare ones hang deep.

sentences.en: And because letters live only at the leaves, no code can be the prefix of another - hover a letter to trace its path from the root.

sentences.en: The leaves, top to bottom, spell what a decoder does when it reaches one.

blocks.html_en: HPACK ships one fixed Huffman code for header text, its frequencies baked into the RFC from real header corpora captured a decade ago, so both ends of a connection always agree on it. Lowercase letters and digits sit near the top of the tree at 5–7 bits; rare bytes hang thirty levels deep. Typical header text comes out around 6 bits per byte. Now notice the property the tree structure gives you for free: no codeword can be the beginning of another, because symbols only live at the leaves. So the bit stream needs no delimiters at all. Read bits until they trace a path to a leaf - that's your symbol. Start again from the root. The stream carries its own boundaries, provided you start at the right place.

sentences.zh: 所以比特流根本不需要分隔符。

blocks.html_en: nghttp2 does something much better, and has since 2014: it decodes with a precomputed finite-state machine. A decoder mid-stream can only be in finitely many states - one per internal node of the Huffman tree, and HPACK's canonical tree has exactly 256 of them, so the state fits in one byte. You can precompute, for every (state, next-n-bits) pair, where you end up and which symbols (if any) you emit along the way. Decoding becomes: take the next n bits, index a table, maybe write a byte, repeat. No bit-buffer, no branching on code lengths.

sentences.en: nghttp2 does something much better, and has since 2014: it decodes with a precomputed finite-state machine.
sentences.zh: nghttp2 做得更好，自 2014 年以来一直如此：它使用预先计算的有限状态机进行解码。

QUICHE's Huffman kernel is slower than nghttp2's FSM, but the bulk of the difference sits above the decoder: HttpHeaderBlock and the layers of representation and bookkeeping each decoded header passes through cost a consistent 20–30 µs per request more than nghttp2's path, on every host we measured. 工程2020年8月4日阅读时间268分钟

Envoy 版本提升使客户损失了 20% 的 HTTP/2 吞吐量。 这条线索穿过两个编解码器、一堆火焰图以及隐藏在每个标头内的霍夫曼代码。

德米特里·伊利耶夫斯基

联合创始人兼首席技术官

不久前，我们对客户的一个专用代理进行了例行 Envoy 升级。 相同的配置、相同的流量和 CPU 图表增加了大约五分之一。 这种图表可以为您赢得没有议程的日历邀请，因此我们决定先行一步并开始深入研究。

对分版本指向 Envoy v1.34，Envoy 将其默认 HTTP/2 编解码器从 nghttp2 切换为 Google 的 oghttp2。 我们并不是第一个注意到的：自该版本以来，用户报告了 15-25% 的延迟回归，而 v1.37.0 最终恢复了默认设置，源代码中的评论承诺“一旦性能与 nghttp2 一致”，将再次尝试。 这解决了我们的客户问题。 它并没有消除我们的好奇心。 为什么不对齐？ HTTP/2 编解码器到底把时间花在了什么事情上？

这篇文章就是调查。 在续作中，我们会让快速编解码器变得更快，但首先要注意的事情。

最好的编解码器，最差的编解码器

Envoy 在运行时标志后面有两个 HTTP/2 实现，尽管没有火焰图，没有人能说出哪个是哪个：

  • nghttp2 - Tatsuhiro Tsujikawa 的 C 库，自 2013 年以来的 HTTP/2 主力，也是 Envoy 的原始编解码器。 精益 C 结构，调用者提供的缓冲区。
  • oghttp2 - 来自 QUICHE 系列的 Google C++ 编解码器，它与 HTTP/3 堆栈共享代码。 它在 v1.34 中成为 Envoy 的默认设置，也是回归报告开始的时候。

我们对四种微架构（Intel Sapphire Rapids、AMD Zen 4、AWS Graviton4、Google Axion）进行了基准测试。 简单设置：同主机环回（h2load → Envoy → Go h2c 后端，或 Envoy 服务 direct_response），每个进程固定到不相交的物理核心，Envoy 处于 --concurrency 1，因此 RPS/core 是一个纯粹的 CPU 效率数字。

用户报告几乎完全重现：在每台主机上，在大量标头代理流量上，nghttp2 比 oghttp2 提高了 15-25% RPS/核心，而在大量连接流失情况下，则提高了 7-19%。 因此，回归是真实的、可移植的，并且存在于编解码器中的某个位置。 是时候打开配置文件了。

PSA

如果您自己构建 Envoy，请检查您的优化标志。 Envoy 的 .bazelrc 不默认为 -c opt - 一个普通的 bazel 构建 //source/exe:envoy-static 会生成一个快速构建（调试）二进制文件，该二进制文件看起来功能齐全，并且每个核心的基准测试比 -c opt 的相同源慢 15–32 倍。 这篇文章中的每个数字都来自 -c opt 构建。 我们以令人尴尬的方式发现了这一点。

HTTP/2 编解码器的工作场所

两种编解码器的火焰图都由相同的工作主导：标头解压缩。 每个跨代理的 HTTP/2 请求到达时其标头都已压缩，代理必须撤消该操作（每跳两次、解码并重新编码），然后才能路由任何内容。 每个请求需要几百个字节的工作量，听起来没什么，除非你将其相乘：每个核心每秒有数万个请求，每个请求有十多个标头字段，因此每个字段的解码路径每秒运行几十万次。

压缩方案是 HPACK (RFC 7541)：两种机制一起工作。 第一个是索引：固定的 61 项静态表涵盖通用标头（:method: GET 是单个字节），双方维护最近看到的标头字段的同步动态表 - 所以第二次发送 cookie: session=abc... 它花费一两个字节，而不是字面上的千字节。 第二种机制处理所有不能被索引命中的事情：文字字符串是霍夫曼编码的。 首次标头、唯一值（请求 ID、令牌、广告供应商在每个请求上轮换的 cookie）以及跨新连接的大部分内容都会通过霍夫曼路径。 边缘的代理看到很多新的连接和很多独特的值，所以这条路径很热门。

两分钟的霍夫曼编码之旅

1951 年，罗伯特·法诺 (Robert Fano) 为麻省理工学院信息论课程的学生提供了一个选择：参加期末考试，或者就他提供的问题写一篇学期论文。 其中一个问题听起来太简单了，不值得评分——给定一组符号以及每个符号出现的频率，找到它们最有效的二进制代码。 法诺没有提到他和克劳德·香农（是的，克劳德·香农）都解决了这个确切的问题，但只得到了近似值。 一位名叫大卫·霍夫曼（David Huffman）的研究生选择了这张试卷，并为此苦苦挣扎了几个月，据他自己说，当解决方案浮出水面时，他刚刚将笔记扔进垃圾桶，开始准备考试。

在他之前的每个人都是从上到下构建代码，将符号集分成两半。 霍夫曼颠倒了它：从底部开始 - 取出两个最稀有的符号，将它们合并为一个，重复直到剩下一棵树。 稀有符号最终会在树的深处带有长代码；频繁的符号最终会变得浅而短。 事实证明，学期论文的结构是最优的1。 七十五年后，它出现在 JPEG、gzip、MP3（对于孩子来说，这就像 Spotify，但没有广告）以及互联网上的每个 HTTP/2 标头中。

HPACK 为标题文本提供了一个固定的霍夫曼代码，其频率从十年前捕获的真实标题语料库中融入 RFC，因此连接的两端始终一致。 小写字母和数字位于树顶部附近的 5-7 位；稀有字节悬挂三十层深。 典型的标头文本约为每字节 6 位。 现在请注意树结构免费为您提供的属性：没有代码字可以是另一个代码字的开头，因为符号只存在于叶子上。 所以比特流根本不需要分隔符。 读取位，直到它们追踪到一片叶子的路径——这就是你的符号。 重新从根源开始。 只要您从正确的位置开始，河流就有自己的边界。

它还会告诉您成本在哪里。 编码是表查找和位附加。 解码就是这样走：左为 0，右为 1，在叶子处发出，跳回根 - 对于 HPACK 的代码，每个输出字节平均有约 6 个相关的分支和加载步骤，这对于 cookie 的一个字符来说是很多机器。

这是标头值的编码部分 - 逐个字符地进行编码，并观察代码打包成字节，而不考虑字节边界：

nghttp2 做得更好，自 2014 年以来一直如此：它使用预先计算的有限状态机进行解码。 解码器中流只能处于有限多个状态 - 霍夫曼树的每个内部节点一个，而 HPACK 的规范树正好有 256 个状态，因此状态适合一个字节。 您可以预先计算每个（状态、下一个 n 位）对的最终位置以及沿途发出的符号（如果有）。 解码变成：获取接下来的 n 位，索引一个表，也许写入一个字节，重复。 没有位缓冲区，没有代码长度分支。

下面的机器根据标准 RFC 7541 代码解码示例标头值，每次查找读取两位，以便整个状态表适合屏幕。 穿过它——桌子和树是同一件事，但穿着不同的衣服：

nghttp2 正是使用 4 位块运行这台机器：每个输入字节两次查找 256 个状态 × 16 个半字节值的表 - 16 KiB，它舒适地位于 L1 缓存中。 有效性检查（HPACK 要求填充为全 1，嵌入的字符串结尾符号是错误）合并到相同的查找中。 这是一个真正出色的工程 - 这也是 nghttp2 的 HPACK 路径配置文件如此平坦的原因之一。

那么oghttp2的Huffman解码器一定是问题所在，对吧？

这是我们的假设，但资料显示没有。 QUICHE 的 Huffman 内核比 nghttp2 的 FSM 慢，但大部分差异位于解码器之上：在我们测量的每台主机上，HttpHeaderBlock 以及每个解码标头经过的表示和簿记层的成本比 nghttp2 的路径多出一致的 20-30 µs 每个请求。 有一个项目很突出：解码器通过 std::string::push_back 发出符号，一次一个字节，并且在标头饱和运行中，仅该调用就消耗了 x86 主机上所有 Envoy CPU 的 13-20%。

您可以在源代码中看到它的形状。 解码器的热循环将每个解码的字符分别交给 std::string ：

每个push_back都是一次容量检查和可能的标题文本的每个字节的重新分配。 然后，一旦一个值被完全解码，每个标头都会在 Envoy 看到它之前经过哈希映射查找和竞技场副本：

单独来看两者都是完全合理的 C++。 在每个标头字段运行一次的路径上（每个核心每秒数十万次），重新分配检查、映射查找和复制总共需要 20-30 µs（配置文件显示），而 nghttp2 的解码器写入调用者提供的缓冲区并继续前进。

公平地说，oghttp2 的框架和会话层比 nghttp2 便宜——在标头文本不再占主导地位的情况下（现实标头、直接响应、无代理），oghttp2 获胜 8-13%。 编解码器并不是到处都很慢。 但是代理的工作描述是头重的，而在头重的流量上，管道税埋葬了框架的胜利。

修复上游需求是从解码字节到标头块的更精简的路径，这是比任何单个热循环更深入的重构。 这大概就是 Envoy 默认值向后翻转而不是向前翻转的原因。

修复

对于我们和我们的客户来说，修复过程非常无聊：

  • Envoy 1.37+：你完成了； nghttp2 再次成为默认值。
  • Envoy 1.34–1.36：设置 envoy.reloadable_features.http2_use_oghttp2：false。 它是一行运行时配置，对于大多数代理 HTTP/2 流量来说，它的 RPS/核心价值为 15–25%。

我们在我们的车队中滚动了旗帜，客户的图表后退，所以日历邀请从未到来（暂时）。 翻转运行时标志比重构标头管道要好得多，因此感谢 Envoy 团队留下的逃生舱口。

结论

编解码器默认值是性能更改。 小版本的 Envoy 改进将我们客户的 CPU 费用改变了 20%，而没有影响线路上的任何一个字节。 如果您操作代理，请对您实际发布的版本进行基准测试。 不过，生成代表实际生产流量的负载可能很棘手，我们稍后会详细介绍。

在优化之前进行分析。 我们确信霍夫曼解码器是罪魁祸首，而火焰图却指向了弦乐管道。 如果有的话，解码器是这两种编解码器中最好的部分。

标头解压是一个很大的工作量。 每个请求几百个字节，每个请求十几个标头字段，每个核心每秒数万个请求，每跳两次 - 算术很快就不再有趣了。 HTTP/2 尝试节省带宽确实会降低 CPU 使用率。 权衡和所有...

不过，当我们在那里时，我们一直盯着 nghttp2 的 n=4 表以及 nghttp2 作者和朋友在 2017 年发表的一篇论文，其中说你可以一次读取整个字节 - 如果你愿意支付一个十六倍大的表。 该交易是否能在与 CPU 缓存接触后继续存在，将在下一篇文章中讨论。 敬请关注。
